text: provides details of the trials with basalt fiber. Basalt fiber rovings of three variants were received from Mafic. These rovings were mounted in the feed roller station. PVC tubing was used to route each roving individually to the cutting head, Figure 45. Figure 46 illustrates the fitting of the PVC tubing to each section of the cutting module (14 ends). The updated GUI for SMC-V2 is shown in Figure 47. Figure 45. (Left) Basalt fiber rovings on feed stand; (Right) PVC tubing leading from feed rolls to the SMC cutting module(s) Figure 46. Close up view of the PVC tubing fitting to each cutting roll (similar to that of glass fibers) 37 Figure 47. Updated GUI for the SMC-V2. Several menus were updated for additional intuitive inputs Figure 48. Evidence of uniform cutting of the basalt rovings. Each of the 14-ends are accurate in their cut length (see red line drawn across the cut ends) 38 Figure 49. Cut basalt fiber rovings, before and after air blast. Some of the sizing on the basalt fiber constrained the roving from filamentizing. With air blast the rovings were filamentized. Figure 50. Fiber weight fraction consistency check. We dialed in a certain inches of cut fiber per foot of travel. We targeted 20 wt% SMC. Cut fibers were collected in the tray as shown. The weight was 155-160 g on a consistent basis which amounted to the target 20 weight percent SMC. The cut quality was excellent as evidence from the cut line, Figure 48. Figure 49 illustrates the cut rovings some of which remained as roving, i.e. did not disperse. With air blast some of the basalt rovings were able to disperse as shown on Figure 49 (right). Figure 50 was the fiber fall down weight consistency check as discussed earlier. 39 Statistical evaluation of fiber length We collected about 6 layers of 18”x24” gravity drop fiber lay down of 0.5” length fibers as shown in Figure 51. These were used to investigate fiber morphology, fiber diameter, length and in-plane uniformity. Figure 52 shows the ½” and 1” fibers collected respectively. The variation of these are visually represented in Figure 53. Figure 51. Collection of set amount of fibers in 18”x24” cardboard. This enables evaluation of fiber lay down and uniformity of the SMC formation in-plane Figure 52. Batches of 1” and ½” collected for fiber length and width analysis Figure 53.. 1” and ½” chopped basalt fiber 40 Figure 54. (Left) 1” basalt fiber cut section; (Right) 0.5” basalt fiber cut section Figure 54 illustrates the cross-section of the 1” and ½” fibers. The mean diameter of the 1” fibers was 17.86 m while those from 0.5” were 16.24 m as summarized in Table 4. Overall the cut quality was fairly similar in both, however the ½’ fibers showed no build-up of fiber residue on the cross-section, i.e. they were very clean in appearance.
